$comment: LEVEL 3 -- DAGAT. Lolo's lines, and the apo's own at the two forks.
⚠ NO LINE MAY NAME A DRAWABLE CLASS, and this level is where that rule is hardest.
Seventeen of the fifty are things you would reach for writing about the sea: fish,
shark, octopus, crab, sea turtle, penguin, frog, sun, cloud, sailboat, submarine,
flashlight, sword, axe, cannon, boomerang, anvil. The check is word-boundary and
case-insensitive, over text AND choice_label, and run_level3_audit.gd runs it.
The fun facts in the coral field belong to the NON-drawable set on purpose -- jellyfish,
starfish, clam, seaweed, urchin -- which is both the design's instruction and the only
way a field of sea creatures can be written at all.
WHAT IS NOT HERE YET: the two lore scenes in full, and the island. They are deferred
with the routes that carry them, and the hooks they will need are not authored in
advance -- an unreachable line is an audit failure, not a placeholder.

lines.text: She painted this one standing about where you are. She told me the water here never looked the same way twice, and she was going to keep at it until it did.
There is something in the wet sand, apo. It has been catching the morning since we came over the dune.
No counting down any more. Hold a shape as long as you like — but it drinks the whole time you are holding it.
Not because you drew it badly. I could not tell it apart from something else, and I would rather say so than guess at you.
There. That one I am sure of.
Feel that? It is going down already. It will not stop going down until you are yourself again.
Her old one gave you a moment and took it back. This one gives you as long as you can pay for. I am not sure yet which of those is kinder.
That is the whole of it, then. She never painted the far side, so I do not know what is standing on it.
Two ways across that I can see. Something that can **swim** will take you under it.
Or that bangka up on the sand. It is too heavy for the two of us — but something that can **carry** a load could dig it out and drag it down to the water. Or something heavy enough to shove it.
So. Over it, or under it?

lines.speaker: apo
lines.text: I will take the bangka. Something strong can drag it down to the water.

lines.speaker: apo
lines.text: I will go under it. It is faster and I can see where I am going.
There she goes. Somebody left that and never came back for it. Get in, apo — I will sit at this end and keep out of your way.
Go on then. I will keep up. I am not carrying anything any more, so it is easy for me.
That one has the back for it. Put it to the bangka, apo.
There — it is loose. Now put your weight behind it, apo, all the way down to the water.
Ha! It moved. Pick it up and do that again — it is a long way down to the water.
Wait. Wait. Do you see how it is going — back and forth over the same stretch, over and over? It is not hunting us. It has lost something.
It cannot see, apo. Not a thing. And there is something about its eyes that I know and cannot put down.
Something that can throw **light** would show it where to look. Something that can **strike** would make it stop.
Or nothing at all. It cannot see you either — keep out of the bright and it will never know you went by.
It cannot see. So what do we do about that?

lines.speaker: apo
lines.choice_label: I will show it where to look.
lines.text: I will show it where to look. It has been at this a long time.

lines.speaker: apo
lines.text: I will go around it. It is not looking for me.

lines.speaker: apo
lines.choice_label: I will put myself between it and you.
lines.text: I will put myself between it and you. It is big and it is frightened and I do not trust it.
Home. It had been going over that same stretch for who knows how long, looking for the way back, and it only needed somebody to hold something up. Oh — apo. It is giving you something.
Good. Quiet. Keep going and do not turn round.
It is still back there, still going over the same stretch. It will be there when we are gone.
It has had enough. Let it go, apo — let it go. It never knew you were there. That is the part I want you to keep.
And whatever it was searching for, it has taken with it. Down into the dark. We will never know what it was.
Look — it turned to it. It follows the light, apo. Lead it home.
There is a hollow in the rock under the first beach, where we came in. I would wager that is where it lives. Bring it back across, and keep the light where it can see it.
There. In the sand, where the light is catching it. That is the next one.
I should tell you the rest of it, before you go on. It happened out there, past where we came in. An afternoon like any other.
I did not get to say anything to anybody. That is the part I would change, if I were allowed to change one part.
And your lola kept painting. This same water, from that same stretch of sand, over and over.
Every one of them came out a little further from what it looks like. She does not always know me now, apo. She still knows which end of the handle to hold.
This is where I stop.
Past here I do not remember. I was not there for it, so there is nothing of me in it to walk through — you would be going on alone whether I came or not.
Go on, apo. I will be in the parts I know.
That one has no heart and no brain and it has been down here longer than anything else. It simply is, and it has never needed to be more.
Turn it over some time. Hundreds of little feet, all of them walking. Take an arm off it and it grows another.
It shuts when the light changes. That is the whole of its opinion about the world, and it has never once been talked out of it.
Hold onto that if a current takes you, apo. It is anchored better than you are.
Do not. I am serious. Do not.
All of this is alive. Every bit of it. It looks like stone because it builds in stone, the way a town does.
Look up. That is the whole top of the world from down here. Not much to it, is there.
Somebody lost that. Things down here belong to whoever lost them, and nobody comes to argue.
Your lola sat out on that sand for a week trying to get this colour. She said the water would not hold still for her.
She could name every one of these. I only ever learned the ones she told me twice.
Row. Do not fight it — let the water carry some of the work, it is going that way anyway.
You are sitting where I sat. I did this stretch a hundred times and never once looked at it properly.
It was out past here. Further than you have been. An ordinary afternoon — that is the part nobody believes, and it is the only part that matters.
I went over and I did not come up. There is no more to it than that. Nothing to see coming, and I have had a long time to look for one.
Listen to the water on the hull. Your lola used to say it sounded like somebody humming in the next room.
Keep rowing, apo. I am glad you are here and I would rather you did not stop.
Stop. Stop rowing — look down.
Something long went under us. It is going round and round on the same stretch, the way a person does when they have lost something in the house.
Keep going. I can talk and you can swim, it is easier that way round.
Your lola was never the same after. I want to be careful how I put that.
She kept painting. The same water, from the same stretch of sand, year on year.
Now she does not always know me. She still knows which end of the handle to hold.
Look at the light coming down through all of that. She tried to get it right every summer and never once said she had.
And you will not be alone down there, apo. Pawikan, dikya, pugita, whole schools of bangus. If you like, draw yourself as one of them and swim the way they do.
Bangus! The whole country chose that one as its own, apo. Raised in the ponds of Pangasinan and Bulacan, and grilled at every fiesta from here to Mindanao.
A pawikan. Five of the world's seven kinds swim in our seas, and they come back to the very beach they hatched on to lay their eggs.
Dikya. Mind the long threads, apo, they sting. I learned that the hard way once, wading at Bantayan.
Pugita! Three hearts and blue blood. It can change its colour quicker than you can blink, and squeeze through any gap wider than its beak.
Apo! Now they are all upset with you. Everything with a sting or a beak is coming for you. Only the bangus will not bother.
Oh. Oh, apo. It was only living here.
Another one. I wish you would not. They were here long before any of us.
Please, apo. That is enough. The sea is not ours to empty.
...I do not want to watch this any more.
Enough! Up you come, apo. Up, and leave them be.
There, under all that sand. Somebody's lost hook, and still sharp.
With that and a line you could sit in the bangka and see what is down there. Your lola's father did it every morning off this beach.
Let it sink, apo. Something will come and look. When it bites, wind it in, and do not let it rest.
There, it has snapped. Five is good going for an old hook. Let the sea keep it.
Bangus on the line! They are full of little bones. The cooks in Dagupan take every one out by hand with tweezers. Back you go, little one.
Gently, gently. The pawikan is protected by law here, so we look, and we let it go. They were swimming these seas before there were people to watch them.
Careful how you hold that. Some dikya in our waters glow in the dark; the old fishermen used to steer home by them at night.
A pugita! In the Visayas they hang them to dry on bamboo racks along the shore. This one goes back where it came from.
Another one! Look at it, and let it go, apo.
Back on the shore, apo. The tide brought you home.
The sea again. Listen to it — it has been waiting for you.
You keep coming back to the water. She was the same.
From the mountains to the sea! Mind the salt, apo — it gets everywhere.

lines.speaker: apo
lines.text: It is so flat here after all those terraces.
Flat on top. Underneath, it is deeper than any mountain is tall.
Still humming the fiesta drums? Out here the waves keep a slower beat.

lines.speaker: apo
lines.text: Two steps forward, one step back... like the tide.
Just like the tide. You are learning, apo.
Last time you took the bangka out. Will you try the water itself today?
Last time you went down under the waves. The bangka is still waiting on the sand.
Last time you stood between me and the deep. Brave. Perhaps there is a kinder way.
Did you know, apo? The Philippines has more than seven thousand islands. Seven thousand six hundred and forty-one, at the last count.

lines.speaker: apo
lines.text: Have you been to all of them?
Not even close. Some are so small they vanish at high tide.
These seas are some of the richest on Earth, apo. Scientists say more kinds of reef life live in Philippine waters than almost anywhere else in the world.
See the bamboo arms on each side of the bangka? Those are outriggers. They are why it does not tip over in rough water.
Long ago our ancestors crossed these seas in boats called balangay. One dug up in Butuan is more than a thousand years old.
The old Visayans told of the bakunawa — a great sea serpent that rose from the deep to swallow the moon.

lines.speaker: apo
lines.text: Swallow the MOON?
So the people banged pots and pans until it spat the moon back out. That is how they explained an eclipse.
They say there were once seven moons in the sky, and the bakunawa swallowed six of them. The last one is the one the people protected.
Far south, in the Sulu Sea, there is a reef called Tubbataha. It is so precious that visitors may only come a few months of the year.
In Donsol, the gentle butanding comes to feed — the biggest creature in these seas, and it lives on the tiniest things in the water.
The fishers there used to hunt it. Now they guide people to swim beside it instead.
Last time you took the bangka over. Will you go under, this time?
Last time you went under. The bangka is still waiting on the sand.
You have crossed both ways now. Choose whichever feels right.
Last time you showed it where to look. Will you try another way today?
Last time you slipped around it. Perhaps face it, this time?
Last time you put yourself between us and it. There may be a kinder way.
You have met it every way there is. Choose what your heart says.
